newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia to face obstacles in meeting export targets.
newsitem.headline: Serbia to face obstacles in meeting export targets.

text.p: More state help is needed to achieve plans to boost 1997 exports by 42 percent and imports by 20 percent, while keeping the trade gap close to $2 billion, businesses said on Thursday.
In 1996, Serbian exports stood at $1.743 billion and imports balooned to $3.81 billion, the Chamber of Commerce said in its report.

Agriculture and food processing industry, metal processing, ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy as well as chemical industry were the largest exporters, selling goods for $1.387 billion, making up for almost 80 percent of total Serbian exports.
Germany, Republika Srpska, Italy, Macedonia, Russian Federation and Greece were the largest Yugoslav trading partners.

Head of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce Vlajko Stojiljkovic insisted Serbia needed to regain preferential trade status and other concessions from other countries in order to improve its export performance.
"High customs duties make our exports even less competitive," Stojiljkovic said, addressing the gathering of managers of leading Serbian trade companies.
Stojiljkovic said Serbia should first turn to neighbouring markets because their vicinity reduces transport costs, but also to markets in Western Europe, Russia, Ukraine and China.
"Serbia runs a massive trade gap and this economy must do more to sell its products," he said.

Inadequate quality and design of local products, as well as non-aggressive marketing campaigns, mismanagement, high prices and unfair competition made Serbian exports even more uncompetitive, the Chamber of Commerce said in its report.
To achieve an ambitiously set export target of around $2.5 billion, Serbia would need around $200 million in monthly exports, the Yugoslav deputy trade minister Tomislav Milenkovic said.
Restoring ties with the International Monetary Fund, World Bank, World Trade Organisation and other international institutions was a precondition for Serbia to return to world markets.
Stojiljkovic insisted economic cooperation with the world was vital for Serbia to embark on genuine transformation and privatisation, one of the top goals of its 1997 economic policy.
"Privatisation is impossible without bigger foreign presence. Both Serbian and foreign companies must be encouraged to establish some kind of industrial cooperation," Stojiljkovic said.
Businessmen also called on the government to reduce red-tape and provide more subsidies at least for those industries with good sale prospects.
Currently, one export deal needs between 12-15 various licences, an industry source said.

Milena Kostic, representing Vojvodina Chamber of Commerce, said companies asked the government to provide cheaper credits for production and exports, but also hoped to get several credit lines from foreign partners. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
